thread.title: Homeland Security Throws Apple and Amazon a Bone on Hacking Report

author: Barron's
title: Homeland Security Throws Apple and Amazon a Bone on Hacking Report
text:
Getty Images The U.S. Department of Homeland Security says it has no reason not to believe Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and other companies that have denied a Bloomberg Businessweek report that Chinese intelligence services inserted malicious computer chips into their equipment.
"The Department of Homeland Security is aware of the media reports of a technology supply chain compromise," DHS said in a statement over the weekend. "Like our partners in the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre, at this time we have no reason to doubt the statements from the companies named in the story."
On Sunday, Apple upped the ante. Its vice president for information security, George Stathakopoulos, wrote in a letter to Congress that it found no evidence of tampering. "Apple's proprietary security tools are continuously scanning for precisely this kind of outbound traffic, as it indicates the existence of malware or other malicious activity," he wrote. "Nothing was ever found."
Bloomberg, citing more than a dozen intelligence and company sources, reported Thursday that Chinese spies placed tiny spy chips inside motherboards and other equipment used by about 30 companies and U.S. government agencies to gain secret access to internal networks.
Apple suppliers took an $18 billion stock hit after the report.
On Friday, Britain's national cyber security agency, the National Cyber Security Centre, backed Apple and Amazon in their hack denials .
Apple contested the report as soon as it was published, citing its own internal investigations that found no evidence supporting the story's claims. The report is particularly sensitive to Apple and its Chief Executive, Tim Cook, who for years have said that Apple better protects the data of its customers than social media rivals . Their views were highlighted in a Barron's cover story in April.
Apple's stance, in light of recent data breaches that have intensified regulatory scrutiny of Facebook ( FB ), Alphabet 's ( GOOGL ) Google, and Twitter ( TWTR ), was underscored in a Cook interview with Vice News that aired last week , days before the Bloomberg report.
Cook told Vice of Apple's unwavering commitment to "collect as little data as possible" and treat privacy as "one of the most important issues of the 21st century."
